items.q: A 42-year-old patient undergoes an urgent laparotomy for a perforated anterior peptic ulcer. Where in the gastrointestinal tract is this perforation most commonly situated?
items.exp: Over 90% of duodenal ulcers occur in the first part of the duodenum (duodenal bulb). Anterior wall ulcers perforate into the peritoneal cavity causing pneumoperitoneum.
r: Correct. The duodenal bulb (D1) is the most frequent site of peptic ulcers and anterior perforation.
Incorrect. D3 is rarely affected by primary peptic ulcer disease.
Incorrect. Gastric fundus ulcers are uncommon compared to antral and duodenal bulb lesions.
Incorrect. D2 ulcers are much less common.
items.kp: The first part of the duodenum (duodenal bulb) is the predominant site for peptic ulcers, with anterior ulcers perforating into the peritoneum.

items.q: A patient with a deep chronic posterior duodenal bulb ulcer presents with sudden hematemesis and hemorrhagic shock. Which artery coursing directly posterior to D1 was eroded?
items.exp: The gastroduodenal artery descends directly posterior to the first part of the duodenum (D1). Chronic posterior ulcers penetrate into this artery, causing massive gastrointestinal hemorrhage.
r: Correct. Posterior duodenal bulb ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery, causing torrential bleeding.
Incorrect. Splenic artery runs along the superior border of the pancreas towards the spleen.
Incorrect. Left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach.
Incorrect. Superior mesenteric artery courses posterior to the third part of duodenum.
items.kp: Posterior duodenal bulb ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery, leading to massive, life-threatening upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

items.q: Which artery directly supplies the gastric fundus via branches that arise from the splenic artery in the splenorenal ligament?
items.exp: The short gastric arteries (typically 4 to 6 branches) arise from the splenic artery at the splenic hilum and pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the fundus.
r: Correct. Short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery to supply the gastric fundus.
Incorrect. Right gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature.
Incorrect. Left gastroepiploic supplies the upper greater curvature.
Incorrect. Right gastroepiploic supplies the lower greater curvature.
items.kp: Short gastric arteries from the splenic artery supply the gastric fundus and run within the gastrosplenic ligament.

items.q: The third (horizontal) part of the duodenum (D3) is vulnerable to vascular compression in young patients with severe weight loss because it is wedged between which two major vessels?
o: Abdominal aorta and superior mesenteric artery
Inferior vena cava and portal vein
Celiac trunk and common hepatic artery
Left renal vein and splenic vein
items.exp: In superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome, loss of the retroperitoneal mesenteric fat pad narrows the aortomesenteric angle, compressing the horizontal duodenum between the aorta and SMA.
r: Correct. SMA syndrome results from compression of D3 between the abdominal aorta and superior mesenteric artery.
Incorrect. IVC and portal vein are not the compressive clamp in SMA syndrome.
Incorrect. Celiac trunk lies superior to the duodenum.
Incorrect. Left renal vein compression between aorta and SMA causes nutcracker syndrome, not duodenal obstruction.
items.kp: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome compresses the third part of the duodenum between the aorta and the SMA.

items.q: Gastric acid-secreting parietal cells and intrinsic factor-producing cells are concentrated primarily in which anatomical regions of the stomach?
items.exp: Parietal (oxyntic) cells and chief (peptic) cells reside predominantly within gastric oxyntic glands in the fundus and corpus (body) of the stomach.
r: Correct. Parietal cells are densely concentrated in the gastric fundus and corpus.
Incorrect. The antrum and pylorus contain mucus-secreting and gastrin-producing G cells.
Incorrect. The cardia contains predominantly mucus-secreting glands.
Incorrect. The pyloric sphincter is smooth muscle without oxyntic glands.
items.kp: Gastric parietal cells secreting hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor are concentrated in the fundus and body.

items.q: The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), which empties into which part of the duodenum?
items.exp: The ampulla of Vater opens into the posteromedial wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.
r: Correct. The ampulla of Vater empties into the second (descending) duodenum.
Incorrect. The first part is the duodenal bulb.
Incorrect. The third part runs horizontally across the spine.
Incorrect. The fourth part ascends to the duodenojejunal flexure.
items.kp: The major duodenal papilla is located on the posteromedial wall of the descending (second) part of the duodenum.

items.q: During surgical mobilization of the lesser curvature of the stomach, ligation of the left gastric artery requires dissection close to its direct origin from which vessel?
items.exp: The left gastric artery is the smallest and first branch arising directly from the celiac trunk, ascending towards the gastroesophageal junction.
r: Correct. The left gastric artery originates directly from the celiac trunk.
Incorrect. It does not originate directly from the abdominal aorta.
Incorrect. Common hepatic is a sister branch from the celiac trunk.
Incorrect. Splenic is another branch of the celiac trunk.
items.kp: The left gastric artery is a direct branch of the celiac trunk, supplying the lesser curvature and lower esophagus.

items.q: Which anatomical structure suspends the duodenojejunal flexure and serves as the clinical landmark separating the upper and lower gastrointestinal tracts?
o: Ligament of Treitz (suspensory muscle of duodenum)
items.exp: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) attaches the duodenojejunal flexure to the right crus of the diaphragm, defining the boundary between upper and lower GI bleeding.
r: Correct. Ligament of Treitz suspends the duodenojejunal flexure and demarcates upper from lower GI tracts.
Incorrect. Hepatoduodenal ligament forms the free edge of lesser omentum.
Incorrect. Gastrocolic ligament connects stomach to colon.
Incorrect. Falciform ligament attaches liver to anterior wall.
items.kp: The ligament of Treitz suspends the duodenojejunal flexure and demarcates the anatomical boundary between upper and lower GI tracts.

items.q: What unique histological feature characterizes the submucosa of the duodenum, distinguishing it from all other parts of the small intestine?
items.exp: Brunner glands are branched tubuloalveolar glands situated in the duodenal submucosa that secrete alkaline, bicarbonate-rich mucus to neutralize acidic gastric chyme.
r: Correct. Brunner glands in the submucosa are pathognomonic for the duodenum.
Incorrect. Peyer patches characterize the ileum.
Incorrect. Crypts of Lieberkuhn exist throughout the small and large bowel.
Incorrect. Meissner submucosal plexus is present throughout the GI tract.
items.kp: Brunner glands located in the duodenal submucosa secrete alkaline mucus to protect mucosa from gastric acid.

items.q: Which muscle layer of the gastric muscularis externa is unique to the stomach and absent throughout the remainder of the gastrointestinal tract?
items.exp: The stomach muscularis externa consists of three layers: outer longitudinal, middle circular, and an inner oblique layer that assists in mechanical churning of food into chyme.
r: Correct. The inner oblique layer is unique to the stomach muscularis externa.
Incorrect. Middle circular layer exists throughout the GI tract.
Incorrect. Outer longitudinal layer exists throughout the GI tract.
Incorrect. Muscularis mucosae is a separate thin mucosal boundary layer.
items.kp: The stomach uniquely possesses three muscularis externa layers, featuring an inner oblique layer for churning.
